speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Principally, the amendments align the regulatory framework for the media sector with that for the telecommunication sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The Bill also makes related amendments to the Telecommunications Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: I will then bring Members through the two key amendments: firstly, those relating to the ownership and control of key media entities; and secondly, amendments that facilitate regulatory actions by IMDA, together with a number of administrative updates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: As the amendments are technical in nature, let me first set out the background and context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA was established in 2016 through the IMDA Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The observation then was that the lines between how content is produced, how it is carried and how it is consumed were starting to converge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA was formed through the merger of the Info-communications Development Authority and the Media Development Authority to become the single regulator and industry developer for both the telecommunication and media sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA relies on the Telecommunications Act as the main legislation for the telecommunication sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The Telecommunications Act covers the licensing of telecommunication systems and services, as well as competition and consumer interest matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Unlike the telecommunication sector, a few regulatory frameworks come together to form IMDA’s toolkit for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The Broadcasting Act and Newspaper and Printing Presses Act (NPPA) determine who is a broadcasting licensee or a holder of a newspaper permit respectively, and such entities may be specified as regulated persons under the IMDA Act and be subject to the competition and consumer protection framework within it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Therefore, the proposed amendments under this Bill deal primarily with the IMDA Act, that is, the competition and consumer protection aspects of our regulatory framework for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The amendments look at the media market structure and practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: They aim to ensure fair competition and market conduct, and that consumers of media services are protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: These are companies that shape the information environment for our citizens, especially in the age of AI and disinformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Clause 9 of the Bill will replace the existing section 65 of the IMDA Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The intent is to broaden IMDA’s oversight of ownership and control changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This is consistent with the 30% voting control level under the Monetary Authority of Singapore's Take-Over Code as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: With this change, IMDA's approval would now be needed if an entity that is not a regulated person wishes to acquire 30% or more of our Pay TV operators, SingNet or StarHub Cable Vision, for example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This requirement is in place today for the telecommunication sector, where acquisitions by any party, crossing certain thresholds, such as 30% ownership or control of key telecom entities require IMDA's prior approval.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: We are adopting this practice for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: I should add that under the Broadcasting Act and NPPA, a person must not become a substantial shareholder, which is defined in the Companies Act as having not less than 5% of the total votes attached to all voting shares in the company, a 12% controller or an indirect controller of a broadcasting company and newspaper company without the Minister’s prior approval.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: These 5% and 12% thresholds give the Government oversight and control over persons who have significant stakes in our media companies to ensure that these companies are not subject to undue influence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The proposed change under the IMDA Act with the 30% controller threshold will add to these safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA will have the powers to assess such changes with additional market conduct and consumer protection considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Broadly, they consist of amendments to facilitate regulatory actions by IMDA and several administrative updates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Under the current Act, IMDA's powers to give directions to regulated persons is limited to cases where there is non-compliance with competition or consumer protection rules under the IMDA Act and the Telecom and Media Competition Code.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: However, there may be instances where actions of licensees may result in outcomes that are detrimental to consumers or undermine fair market competition, despite there being no breach of the IMDA Act or the Code.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Just to illustrate based on a past telecom sector example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: It is unfair to you, as a consumer, if your provider abruptly changes the price or the terms and conditions of your subscription during the contractual lock-in period to your disadvantage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: To protect consumers, IMDA prohibited such practices in 2015 and could do so quickly through a direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA subsequently formalised the requirements in the Code.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA does not have such powers to act in this manner for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: IMDA will need to first revise and reissue the Code of Practice before it can act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This takes time and consumers will be worse off during the interim period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This Bill also makes a few other amendments that are administrative in nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: First, the new section 65B introduced by clause 9 and the new section 71A introduced by clause 16 of the Bill enable IMDA to obtain specific information to support regulatory decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: These information-gathering powers are to ascertain a person’s equity interests or voting power in a regulated person for the purposes of assessing ownership changes and gather information relating to the potential designation of a media service as an essential resource.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: We recognise that a structural separation is a significant regulatory intervention and it is appropriate that a decision of this gravity is taken at the Ministerial level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This mirrors the existing position in the Telecommunications Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The basis for these powers is meant as a last resort, to eliminate barriers to competition created by the control of bottleneck media resources or the possession of significant market power, after existing and potential regulatory actions by IMDA are deemed to be ineffective to enhance competition and where the Minister is satisfied it is in the public's interest to issue a separation order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: To illustrate, the current definition of “regulated person” in the IMDA Act covers a “newspaper company” for the purposes of section 65.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: A newspaper company is defined in the NPPA as a public company limited by shares in compliance with section 10, which provisions includes, among others, a requirement for all directors to be Singaporean citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This requirement was in place when the NPPA was enacted in 1974.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Other forms of corporate structures could similarly hold newspaper permits and their publications may have similar reach and influence, even if the entities do not fall within the narrow definition of a “newspaper company”, such as having Singaporean citizen-only directors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The updated definition will allow these entities to be captured as regulated persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: On the broadcasting side, the current definition of a regulated person in the IMDA Act covers only holders of broadcasting licences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Structures, like business trusts, that hold broadcasting assets are not covered under the current definition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: We are updating the definition to cover such trust structures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This is aligned with the approach for the telecommunication sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This is a practice informed by our experience with the telecom sector, where international standards have been considered and adapted for setting relevant standards for Singapore, such as the use of standards by the International Telecommunications Union and the European Telecommunications Standards Institute for mobile handsets and terminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: To illustrate, where there are already good industry standards developed by professional bodies or industry associations, IMDA would have powers to require compliance with these industry-developed standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: It avoids duplicate rule-making and it builds on industry buy-in because the rules are ones that industry itself has developed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Fifth, in a similar spirit for our regulations to be practical, clause 9 of the Bill deems it sufficient for persons to notify IMDA, instead of seeking IMDA’s approval, for immaterial transactions to be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The intention is to prescribe transactions which do not have an impact on equity interests or control of voting power held by shareholders of key media entities, for example, due to a transfer of shares between a corporation and its wholly owned subsidiary as part of a corporate restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: This amendment will lighten the regulatory burden and align the approach taken for the telecom sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: Lastly, clause 18 makes related amendments to the Telecommunications Act itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister of Digital Development and Information)
text: The amendments update drafting, terminology and cross-references so that the two Acts use consistent languages and terms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The question before us is not whether these powers are needed but how we ensure they are exercised with clarity, with consistency and with proportionality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I rise in support of this Bill to strengthen competition, protect consumers and ensure that our media ecosystem remains fair, vibrant and resilient.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As chairperson of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Digital Development and Information, allow me to briefly summarise the GPC's approach towards this Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Collectively, members of the GPC recognises the need for Singapore's regulatory framework to evolve alongside the growing convergence of digital platforms, telecommunications and media ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our speeches will focus on three broad themes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, I will focus on ensuring that a stronger regulatory and preemptive powers are matched by stronger safeguards, greater proportionality and clearer regulatory frameworks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, Member Ms Jessica Tan will focus on strengthening fair competition, protecting consumers and ensuring that SMEs and local creators continue to have fair access to essential digital and media resources.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And third, Dr Choo Pei Ling will focus on how market influence today increasingly arises through ecosystem dependencies, platforms and infrastructure, not just ownership alone, and why regulation must therefore become more forward-looking and structurally aware.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Taken together, we support empowering IMDA with the tools necessary to act decisively in a rapidly evolving digital landscape while ensuring these powers are exercised transparently, predictably and proportionately.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And it is on this principle that I would like to begin my speech.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These are structural tools that can shape the market itself.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, we must ask three very practical questions, questions that any business investor or even members of the public would naturally ask.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will decisions be explained clearly and consistently?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And will uncertainty create a regulatory overhang that deters investment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because in Singapore, one of our key strengths is that we are predictable, transparent and rules-based.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Investors are not afraid of regulation, but they need to understand the operating boundaries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They need the confidence that decisions are made consistently and not unpredictably.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Therefore, I would encourage the Ministry to consider providing clearer guidelines and decision frameworks and ensuring transparent reasoning for major decisions and assurance that these powers are applied in a proportionate and consistent manner.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We are moving from regulating behaviour to shaping market structure itself or potentially shaping market itself.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Traditionally, regulators act when something goes wrong, when there is a breach, when there is harm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is a fundamental shift from reactive enforcement to proactive market structure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And with this shift, an important question arises.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Does it have sufficient data and market visibility to identify risk early?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Does it have the economic modelling capability to assess long-term impact?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And does it have the institutional strength to make, explain and defend these decisions, which will undoubtedly be legally challenged?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More importantly, how will IMDA strike the right balance between competition, innovation and media sustainability?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because in a small market, like Singapore, this balance is delicate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Too much intervention may discourage investment and innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Too little intervention may allow dominance to take root.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about addressing market power – who owns, who controls and whether others can compete fairly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The provisions on this Bill deal with ownership structures, access to resources and competitive conduct.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They do not deal with editorial content or journalistic decisions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In fact, we should recognise an important point – a more competitive and contestable media landscape can actually strengthen this ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because when no single player dominates, there is greater diversity of voices, perspective and viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The objective here is to ensure that no one can control the market unfairly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, the assumption that market power can be clearly identified early.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But in digital markets, conditions change very rapidly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Today's dominant player may not remain dominant tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, the assumption that intervention will always lead to better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Sometimes, the outcome may differ from what it was intended.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Thirdly, the assumption that more intervention necessarily leads to more competition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Imagine a digital platform widely used by Singaporeans to access news and content has just gained immense popularity all of a sudden.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A small change is made to its recommendation algorithm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some local publishers, especially the smaller, independent ones, suddenly become less visible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Their viewership drops significantly and within weeks, some may struggle to survive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But the time the harm is clearly visible and proven, it may already be irreversible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In a small market, like Singapore, once it is lost, it is very difficult to be rebuilt.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is why in fast-moving digital markets, waiting for harm to occur is sometimes not an option.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But equally, this example highlights why such powers must be exercised with clear thresholds, strong evidence and careful judgement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, the key question is: how will IMDA distinguish between genuine collaboration and hidden control?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To strengthen confidence, it will be helpful to provide clearer guidelines on safe harbour principles or clarify what constitutes effective control in practice and focus on substantive influence rather than technical relationships.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Under section 61A, IMDA can act in the public interest, even without a breach.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we ensure preemptive action does not become premature action?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To address this, we may consider clear evidentiary thresholds, demonstration of credible and eminent risk, and the possibility of review mechanisms to reassess decisions over time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This ensures that the action is based on real risks, not just theoretical concerns.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill already provides that other measures must have failed or are likely to fail.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we demonstrate that less intrusive options are insufficient?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we ensure accountability in such decisions?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because once exercised, structural separation is difficult to reverse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It reflects a simple but important reality: that in today's digital age, market power can emerge quickly and sometimes, invisibly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we wait too long, the damage may already be done.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But with stronger power must come stronger responsibility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must empower IMDA to act decisively, but we must also ensure it acts predictably and proportionately.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ultimately, this Bill is not about controlling the media, it is about ensuring that no one controls the media unfairly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we get this balance right, we will not only strengthen competition, we will strengthen trust, resilience and diversity in Singapore's ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill is a necessary and timely update to harmonise regulations within a converging digital market.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While the direction of travel is broadly understandable, the Bill does grant the Government significant powers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While it may align with the existing practices in the telecommunication industries to place such powers directly in the hand of the Minister, this also raises important questions about the concentration of decision-making authority within the hands of political officeholders.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: They have far-reaching implications for markets, investors and consumers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore important that such decisions are guided by clear objective criteria and that they be seen to do so.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill does not currently require the detailed publication of reasons for such decisions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Without this, there may be concerns about transparency and predictability.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Businesses need clarity on how decisions are made and the public needs confidence that such powers are exercised in a fair and consistent manner.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We suggest that the Minister should make public a detailed reasoning behind a separation order before one is made.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While this adds procedural flexibility, it does not address a broader structural concern – the absence of an independent appeals body which is not under the executive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In other areas of competition law, appeals are heard by independent tribunals.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This provides a layer of separation between the regulator and adjudicator, enhancing confidence in the system.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Here, both the separation order and the appeal are issued and heard respectively by the executive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While there may be practical reasons for this arrangement, the Government should explain why an independent appeal mechanism is not being adopted, particularly given the increasing complexity of digital market regulation.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill allows for certain regulatory determinations, such as the designation of dominant players to be communicated through private notifications rather than public gazetting.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While this may streamline administration, it reduces public visibility into how market power is assessed and regulated.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In sectors as critical as media and telecommunications, transparency is not merely a procedural matter.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Consumers, competitors and investors all benefit from understanding who holds significant market power and how that power is being managed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Government should, therefore, clarify how it intends to balance efficiency with transparency in implementing these provisions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How will we ensure that the relationship between the regulator and the companies does not become even more opaque and hidden from public view?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill also introduces broad concepts, such as control and essential resources, which underpin many of its new powers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While flexibility is useful in a fast-moving digital landscape, overly broad definitions may create uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Businesses may find it difficult to assess whether routine commercial arrangements fall within the regulatory scope.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, the category of regulated persons can be expanded by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These raises questions about how emerging digital platforms, such as streaming services, will be treated.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Clear guidance will be important to ensure that regulation remains targeted and proportionate, without inadvertently discouraging innovation or investment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill is also framed as promoting competition.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yet in practice, Singapore's media landscape has long been characterised by structural concentration, particularly in sectors, such as free-to-air broadcasting and print.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill clearly strengthens the regulatory tools available to the Government to structure the media industry to promote competition.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, these additional powers granted to the Government by the Bill should not inadvertently result in the further erosion of media pluralism.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We need clear statutory safeguards to ensure these powers are exercised fairly, transparently and in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, notwithstanding my clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We debate this Bill at a critical juncture in the global digital landscape, where infrastructure, platforms and data are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For a small, open nation, like Singapore, our media landscape is not just an industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is where our national stories are told, where perspectives are shaped and where trust is built.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A market dominated by a single player is not merely an economic risk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the power to intervene is also the power to reshape an industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure these powers deliver real benefits to Singaporeans without unintended consequences, I seek clarifications in three areas: affordability, worker protection and opportunities for smaller players.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Heartland families today are navigating rising cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If media markets are not truly competitive, the consumer ultimately pays through bundling, limited choice and rising subscription costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must reduce prices that families actually feel.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill strengthens IMDA's powers over market conduct and structure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But how will these interventions translate into tangible price relief for the average family?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, I note and support the effort under section 65 to reduce regulatory burden by exempting certain immaterial transactions from prior approval.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a significant shift as approval is now required regardless of whether the acquiring party is a media entity or not.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how IMDA will assess such acquisitions, particularly where new entrants may bring innovation and capital but are not traditional media players?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister also clarify how IMDA will ensure that approval processes remain timely and predictable so that we do not inadvertently deter investments that could lower costs through innovation and scale?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are significant interventions that may carry legal and operational costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister assure this House that such powers will be exercised judiciously and that any resulting costs will not ultimately be passed on to consumers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this can promote competition, it may also reduce economies of scale and increase duplication of costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that this power is vested in the Minister rather than IMDA, given the significant impact of such decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how this higher threshold of decision-making will be exercised and what considerations will guide such interventions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry evaluate the trade-off between fostering competition and preserving efficiency so that affordability for households is not compromised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If competition improves on paper but prices do not fall, residents will not feel the benefit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A competitive market must also be an affordable market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our media industry is powered by people: journalists, producers, technicians and increasingly, freelancers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I acknowledge that employment protections fall under the Employment Act and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) guidelines, the interventions in this Bill can have real and immediate consequences for workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how IMDA will work with MOM and unions to ensure that workers affected by such changes are adequately supported and that transitions are managed fairly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Further, under section 65A, IMDA may direct the disposal of business units.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government assessed the potential employment impact of such interventions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will considerations of workforce stability form part of the broader public interest assessment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond immediate restructuring, I would also like to understand the longer-term effects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In an environment where structural interventions are possible, firms may adopt a more cautious approach to long-term workforce commitments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While formal employment protections apply, the practical response may still be a preference for leaner organisational structures and more flexible staffing models.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will increased competition in this sector lead to better jobs, or more fragmented and less secure employment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A more competitive market must also be a more secure job market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A healthy market must also be one that provides stability and dignity for workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, the impact on local small media players and freelancers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These independent creators are vital to innovation, diversity and the vibrancy of our media ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill is rightly targeted at regulated entities and anti-competitive conduct, I seek clarification on whether there may be indirect compliance implications for smaller players who interact with these entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces detailed definitions of control and associate under sections 59 and 60B.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are structured around equity interests and defined relationships.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how this expanded scope will be applied in practice, particularly to avoid unintended capture beyond key media entities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While necessary for enforcement, can the Minister assure that these powers will be exercised proportionately, particularly where smaller businesses or individuals are involved?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am also concerned about barriers to entry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If compliance requirements become complex or uncertain, smaller players may feel compelled to incur legal costs simply to ensure they remain compliant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how, on balance, this results in a net reduction of regulatory burden, particularly for smaller and emerging players?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how IMDA will ensure that such externally developed standards remain robust, transparent and aligned with public interest, particularly where industry interests are involved?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regulation should be a ladder for growth, not a hurdle to entry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In an age of global media consolidation, we must have the tools to ensure that our market remains fair, competitive and resilient.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But residents will not judge this Bill by its legal provisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will opportunities remain open to new and diverse voices?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this Bill focuses on market structure and not content, we should recognise that in the media sector, structure and trust are closely related.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we strengthen regulatory powers, it is important that confidence in editorial independence and the diversity of voices continues to be maintained.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They experience outcomes in their bills, in their jobs and in their opportunities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we strengthen control over the market without delivering clear improvements in affordability, jobs and opportunities, we risk building a system that is more regulated, but not necessarily better for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that as we reshape our media industry, we deliver not just stronger rules, but better outcomes for families, for workers and for the next generation of creators.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The IMDA already regulates both the media and telecommunications sectors.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Drawing on a common framework across both is defensible on efficiency grounds and harmonisation grounds.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the argument goes further than that, because digital delivery has converged, because newspapers and broadcasters now reach audiences over the same networks as telephone companies, the Government says that they should be subject to the same regulatory powers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find this difficult to accept this prima facie without deeper scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The delivery mechanism may be shared, but the nature of what is being regulated is not.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is this: this Bill may not be about the media landscape as it exists today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is about the one that has not yet arrived – a future where genuinely independent media may grow in reach and maturity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And my fear is that this Bill is written to foreclose that future before it has the chance to arrive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The infrastructure – cables, spectrum, exchange points – this is neutral.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a single actor controls it, others are locked out.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Newspapers and broadcasters make editorial choices: what to investigate, what to publish, whose voice to amplify.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power to shape public discourse is categorically different from the power to route a data packet.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A press regulation regime needs press safeguards, editorial independence on the face of the statute, so that the regime cannot reach what a publication chooses to investigate or publish.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Plurality conditions on ownership approvals designed to protect diversity of voice.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Higher proportionality when restricting a press entity than a telecommunications operator.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Independent review on the merits when a media entity is singled out by the executive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It takes the structural toolkit or design for network operators – ownership approvals, proactive directions, separation orders – and applies it to entities that produce speech.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our two major media companies today, SPH Media Trust and Mediacorp, are both Government-linked.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both already within the Government's orbit, whether it is formally or informally.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Extending regulatory powers over entities already in that orbit makes little sense and does not meaningfully change the competitive dynamics.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more significant read of this Bill, and my read, is that this is a pre-emptive measure, not about managing existing players, it is about ensuring that no new actor, perhaps a well-capitalised private investor or a media group with genuine editorial independence, can build a meaningful presence outside the Government's reach.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Think of Apple Daily in Hong Kong, or the Washington Post, both funded by individuals with deep pockets of their own and strong political convictions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Jimmy Lai and Jeff Bezos are not politically neutral figures, but their convictions were their own, not the Government's.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is precisely what made their publications independently powerful.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They could ask hard questions without needing permission from whoever held office.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The designation power in section 59(1) is the instrument for pre-empting that possibility here.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore does have independent media that falls outside the state's orbit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It publishes long-form journalism on Singapore's society, politics and policy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As of October last year, it had around 8,000 paying subscribers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not funded by advertising or any Government-linked body.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It scrapes by because readers choose to pay for serious journalism.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On a wide reading, it may well fall within the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If Jom were ever designated under section 59, all three new powers would apply.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the Minister could order its business transferred to another entity – with compensation the Minister determines, subject to no independent review on the merits.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is not written for Jom as it stands today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is written for what Jom, or another publication like it, might become in 10 years.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A publication with the reach to shape conversations, to hold power to account, and to be read by Singaporeans because it has earned their trust.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the future that I fear this Bill is designed to foreclose.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A future where Singapore has a genuinely independent press – publications that owe their survival to the readers, not to the goodwill of any government and that can ask hard questions of whoever holds power, including us.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So if this is not the Bill's intent, I urge the Government to clarify.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under section 59(1), the Minister may designate any newspaper publisher or broadcasting licensee as a "regulated person" and then bringing it within the scope of all three powers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister selects who is regulated, at their discretion.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The selection is the gateway to everything that follows.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The IMDA may issue proactive directions to regulated persons to ensure fair market conduct, effective competition and simply, "in the public interest".

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That last ground is left undefined, and a direction under that section may require a regulated person to do or refrain from doing anything specified.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no limit on subject matter in the text.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Consultation may be waived whenever IMDA considers it "not practicable or desirable".

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no proportionality requirement and no obligation to give written reasons.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the consultation process on this Bill, two law firms filed responses on these gaps.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The definitions of "control" and "associate" are broad, capturing informal arrangements, oral agreements and trusts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A standard minority investor protection is treated the same as an acquisition of effective control.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may be denied entirely if the Minister finds that anti-competitive conduct took place – a finding the Minister also makes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, there is one decision-maker, at every stage, on every question.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No independent check on the merits of any of it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we debated the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act last year, I raised a structurally similar concern.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In that Bill, the powers at least sat with a statutory Commissioner, not a Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I proposed an appeal to the High Court on three limited grounds.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same structural choice, or at least a similar one, appears here: compulsory restructuring of a media businesses, with the Minister at every decision point and no appeal on the merits available to any Court.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The powers inscribed in this Bill will not belong to this Government alone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They sit on the books for every future Government, every future Minister, in every future Parliament.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parliament should ask itself whether it is comfortable with that, whoever holds power.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without a single direction ever being issued, without a single separation ever being ordered.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These powers do not need to be exercised to do their work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A rational investor who wants to fund serious, independent journalism in Singapore, they will read this Bill and they will ask, "Can IMDA issue a direction to this publication on public interest grounds?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot define in advance and with no proportionality test and no written reasons and no independent appeal on the merits." The answer appears to be yes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister order the business transferred determining compensation unilaterally on the finding of anti-competitive conduct that the Minister himself also makes?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The newsroom does not expand, the publication does not grow.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is how unconstrained statutory powers work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not need to be exercised, they only need to exist in plain language for any investor doing a risk assessment to conclude: not here, not now, not under these conditions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan has also assured us today that this would be used as a matter of last resort.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I have six questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 59 allows the Minister to designate any newspaper publisher or broadcasting licensee as a regulated person on no published criteria.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What criteria will the Government use to determine which entities are designated?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will these criteria be published before any designation is made?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And will the same criteria apply equally to Government-linked and independently owned entities?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, and related, on the scope of designation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A regulated person under section 59 includes the holder of a broadcasting licence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would like the Minister to clarify if this reaches social media companies, including large foreign players with a local presence?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, would blogs, social media accounts, podcasts and so on, be covered?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, will the Government publish the criteria that would govern such designation?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 61A permits IMDA to issue proactive directions simply in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister commit to publishing criteria for when this ground will be invoked?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the Minister issues a separation order under 69A, the Minister may direct transfer to a separate entity which need not be an independent media entity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the structure of Singapore's media market, the realistic candidates for transference are today, Government-linked bodies.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister confirm that the compulsorily separated media business will not be directed to a Government-linked entity without the agreement of the regulated person?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may be denied entirely if the Minister finds anti-competitive conduct under section 69A, a finding that the Minister makes themselves, having already ordered the separation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What principles govern this determination of compensation and what safeguards exist to, against the finding being used to deny compensation to an entity whose business the Minister has already compelled, to transfer?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Following separation, the new entity must reapply for a newspaper permit under section 69A, 3B(2).

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government decides whether to grant the new one.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At one level, this is a technical update to thresholds, approvals and enforcement tools.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But at a deeper level it is about how Singapore regulates market power in a system where influence is increasingly exercised through dependency, not just ownership.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That distinction matters because in a converged digital ecosystem, control does not always appear at the point of acquisition.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It can accumulate quietly through minority stakes, infrastructure dependencies and control over distribution systems that sit beneath what consumers actually see and once embedded, these structures are difficult to reverse.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The media regulation we face today is undergoing a crucial shift.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the past, we understood market structure primarily through the lens of "who owns the company." However, in today's digital ecosystem, influence often stems not from ownership itself, but from "dependencies" within the system.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When a platform, infrastructure, or data distribution channel becomes irreplaceable, market power may already be concentrated within the system, even without obvious monopolistic practices.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, the key shift in regulatory thinking is: not just looking at "who owns," but identifying "who is becoming irreplaceable" earlier.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we only intervene after problems emerge, we often miss the opportunity to adjust the structure.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This reflects a necessary recognition that market influence today is not confined within sectoral boundaries.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Capital is cross-platform, strategy is ecosystem-based and influence can be indirect but still structurally significant.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These effects are often not separable at the point of approval; they emerge over time.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is an exceptional intervention that can reshape market structure itself.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The question is therefore not only about authority but about regulatory signalling.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Not to constrain discretion, but to strengthen predictability in a domain where investment confidence depends on clarity of risk boundaries.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the reconsideration mechanism, I note the "either-or" structure between IMDA reconsideration and Ministerial appeal.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry clarify the policy intent behind this design?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is the primary objective speed, finality, or avoidance of parallel processes?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because the structure of review pathways ultimately shapes how regulatory legitimacy is perceived, not just how quickly decisions are resolved.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill adopts broad, technology-neutral definitions of "control" and "essential resource".

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is appropriate in a rapidly evolving environment.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because interpretability affects not only compliance, but also investment timing and market entry decisions.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is a trade-off the system is making.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In that context, would the Ministry consider over time, publishing non-binding guidance or anonymised aggregated decision patterns, particularly around recurring assessment factors and common risk indicators?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would not reduce discretion, but it would improve predictability where regulatory patterns are already structurally consistent.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both are indispensable." Mr Speaker, Singapore is now managing a new form of concentration risk, not only in ownership structures, but in dependency relationships embedded across platforms, infrastructure and digital distribution systems.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regulation must therefore do two things at once: remain firm enough to intervene early and remain clear enough for good actors to navigate confidently.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In plain terms, it strengthens oversight of ownership control and strengthens IMDA's ability to act when market conduct harms competition or consumers.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the past, telecommunications could be understood as infrastructure and carriage.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Media was understood as content and publishing, but today consumers do not experience them separately.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A citizen watches news, entertainment and commentary over data networks.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Digital platforms operate across both infrastructure and content ecosystems, and a small number of major gatekeepers can influence both access and visibility.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In such an environment, if our frameworks remain too fragmented, we create uneven rules for functionally similar activity that can encourage regulatory arbitrage, where firms structure themselves to exploit gaps between regimes rather than compete on service quality, innovation and value.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill's effort to bring media competition and conduct provisions closer to the telco model is therefore a necessary response to technological convergence.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill strengthens IMDA's framework around ownership, control and regulated persons, including powers linked to controllers and essential resources.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It also tightens oversight of significant controls and transactions, including where a party crosses key voting control thresholds.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This matters because media ownership is never just a corporate matter.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It affects the diversity of voices, the resilience of public discourse and the range of perspectives available to citizens in a small and highly connected media market like Singapore's, concentration of ownership or opaque influence can have outsized effects.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, when we review ownership rules, we are asking a wider societal question.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How do we preserve a media environment that remains trusted, diverse and resilient in an age of consolidation and digital concentration?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For the ordinary citizen, this is not abstract.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It affects whether one receives information from a range of credible sources or from an ecosystem that is overly shaped by a few dominant actors.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It affects whether media remains plural enough to support informed citizenship and it affects whether public trust in information ecosystems can be maintained.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In that sense, stronger ownership safeguards are not only about control.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are about protecting the quality of the information space that citizens inhabit every single day.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, these powers must be exercised with clarity and discipline.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In a globalised environment, the framework must be robust without becoming unnecessarily rigid.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The objective is to guard against harmful concentration and opaque influence, while allowing legitimate investment, innovation and sectoral development.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When markets become concentrated, or when certain players can unfairly leverage control over essential resources, harm flows directly to our citizens.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Anti-competitive conduct can lead to fewer choices, weaker incentives to innovate, poorer service quality and higher costs over time.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It can also create barriers for smaller or newer players, reducing dynamism and entrenching incumbents.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Competition policy is not merely about punishing bad behaviour.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is about preserving healthy market conditions so that consumers are not disadvantaged by structural imbalances.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And in the media space, competition issues are not just economic.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They can shape who gets distribution, whose content reaches audiences and which firms survive.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Industry players will need clear signals about the thresholds, obligations and enforcement expectations.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The public, too, should be able to see that these interventions are designed not to over-regulate, but to preserve fairness, openness and resilience in a converged digital landscape.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these observations, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I declare my interest as Assistant Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Stricter merger approval requirements, clearer direction powers for IMDA against anti-competitive conduct and a more coherent framework as our telecoms, broadcasting and newspaper sectors converge are timely and important.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And I would like to raise three areas where we can strengthen the worker dimension so that the sector remains competitive, while our workers and PMEs have confidence through change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That prior-approval gate is also the right point to look beyond market structure and ask what the transaction could mean for the workers and workforce impacted and affected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Major consolidation in the infocomm and media sector often comes with restructuring, role rationalisation and changes to how work is organised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this sector, many of these job roles are undertaken by professionals, managers and executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They include engineers, operators, content and production professionals and thus the impact on livelihoods can be significant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is why worker confidence and timely support matter in any major sector restructuring.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important that the powers in this Bill are exercised in ways that are pro-competition and pro-worker, so that a "market win" does not become a "social loss".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In that spirit, can the Minister consider whether IMDA’s assessment framework should formally incorporate workforce impact alongside market competition impact?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is particularly important as in the course of consolidation, employees may be moved to a different employing entity involving changes to their roles and job scope when the new parent group's competitive model is built on doing more with fewer people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore’s labour management relations are stable and our tripartite framework has served us well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My ask is that we extend that spirit more deliberately into sector consolidation processes so that where livelihoods are affected, issues, like collective agreement continuity and union representation, are addressed early, and the workers' voice remains present.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this spirit, I have three questions which I hope the Senior Minister of State can address.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, would the Government consider putting in place a formal tripartite platform for the infocomm and media sector, so that the workforce issues arising from restructuring and consolidation can be addressed early and systematically?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to work with the Government and industry as a constructive partner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are not asking to oppose change but for clarity, contemporaneous communication, equitability and assurance so that impacted workers will not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope today's debate helps move us in that right direction.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I support this Bill because it will help Singapore keep pace with how quickly the digital and media world is evolving.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These changes recognise that influence in today’s media environment no longer comes only from equity stakes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It increasingly arises from data access, exclusive content arrangements, platform prioritisation and algorithmic control.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill ensures that IMDA has the tools to address these realities in a fair and future-ready way.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A key thrust of this Bill is strengthening fair competition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendments in section 2 broadens the definitions of "arrangement", "control" and "essential resources" so IMDA can act when a company uses its position – formally or informally – to block others from entering the market.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This matters, because in the digital world, dominance can form very quickly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A platform can become the default choice for millions almost overnight.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clearer rules help ensure that competition remains healthy and that companies compete on quality and innovation, and not locking others out.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill ensures that no single player can accumulate influence in the ways that reduces competition or harm consumers, keeping the market open, diverse and competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: More families now depend on digital services from news consumption to seniors staying connected, children learning online and households streaming entertainment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When one company becomes too dominant, consumers may face higher prices, fewer choices, weaker service quality and unfair practices like being locked into bundles or platforms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While this Bill does not set new standards for service quality or reliability, section 61A allows IMDA to intervene early if anti-competitive conduct threatens the continuity or reliable provision of media services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: SMEs and local creators are vital to our media and digital ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They bring fresh ideas, local stories and innovative services but often face higher barriers when competing with large platforms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The new section 61A strengthens fair access to essential resources, such as content libraries, distribution platforms and advertising inventories.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It empowers IMDA to issue directions to ensure non-discriminatory access and prevents any player from using control as an essential resource to block competitors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This means that smaller players cannot be denied access or priced out simply because a large competitor controls a key resource.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When SMEs can access essential resources fairly, they are more willing to experiment, invest and innovate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This leads to more diverse content, more home-grown digital services and more opportunities for local talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These powers are necessary to address modern forms of influence in a converged media digital environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But at the same time, the breadth of these powers mean that clear guidance and transparent processes will be essential to avoid over-correction, ensure business certainty and to maintain a pro-innovation environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while the expanded definitions in section 2 are important to capture modern forms of influence, their breadth does introduce risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Companies and investors may become overly cautious about partnerships and innovative business models, for fear of inadvertently triggering regulatory scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Routine commercial arrangements may be perceived as falling within scope, increasing compliance costs and slowing investment decisions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clear guidance on how these definitions will be applied in practice will help maintain a pro-innovative environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But even if it is rarely used, the existence of this power may affect investment decisions if criteria are unclear.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clarity on the circumstances under which structural separation may be considered will give industry confidence that it will be used proportionately and predictably.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It protects consumers and supports SMEs and local creators.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It reinforces a fair, open and diverse digital environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, increased oversight always carries the risk of over correction if applied too broadly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While this Bill might appear technical, it matters because media is not just another industry.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My first point is on aspirations and employment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A media ecosystem that is open and contestable should, in principle, create more opportunities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But this Bill does not directly create those opportunities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Rather, it seeks to prevent a market structure where opportunities become too concentrated in the hands of a few dominant players.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is important because when the market becomes too concentrated, smaller firms might find it harder to enter, new ideas may struggle to find distribution and our young workers might find fewer employers to choose from.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Workers would then have fewer pathways into the industry.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For our young and our workers, this matters because the media content and ecosystem industry today brings work, such as production and design data, advertising technology, communication and platform-facing businesses.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important given our current job climate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We encourage Singaporeans to upskill, sign up for SkillsFuture, stay relevant to industrial needs.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With this Bill, I hope to be able to say to every Singaporean, if you choose to build your skills in this sector, Singapore is working to keep the media and ecosystem open, contestable and future-ready.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, there is a tension that we must manage carefully.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill introduces strong controls over ownership, voting power, acquisition, effective control and the use and sharing of essential resources.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These powers may be necessary to prevent dominance and protect public interest, but if applied without sufficient proportionality, they may create uncertainty for legitimate growth or even fundraising.
